review.headline: Missed tactical shots lead to a rapid collapse on the kingside

sections.text: You opened with an active setup against the Sicilian, developing smoothly with 7.Bc4 and 8.Bb3. After Black pushed 9...e5, the light-square outpost on d5 became a major target. When Black castled with 10...O-O, you had an immediate opportunity to seize control with 11.Bd5.

Instead, you opted for 11.Qd2, which set up a pin against d6 along the d-file. Black lashed out on the queenside with 11...b4, and after 12.Ne2, Black blundered with 12...Nxe4. You had a winning tactic with the engine's 13.Qd5, creating a fork against the knight on e4 and the rook on a8. Capturing with 13.Qxb4 missed that shot and let Black back into the fight.

Black pushed aggressively with 17...e3, challenging your setup. Rather than capturing with 18.Bxe3 to keep your pieces coordinated, you played 18.fxe3. This left your bishop on h6 completely undefended. Black snapped it up with 18...Bxh6, winning a piece and forcing your resignation after 19...Bxe3.

review.turning_point: The decisive moment was 18.fxe3, which left your bishop on h6 unprotected and allowed 18...Bxh6, costing you a piece and the game.
review.focus: Look for double attacks on unguarded pieces, such as spotting the 13.Qd5 fork instead of playing 13.Qxb4.

White left their king in the center too long, but you missed a cleaner tactical blow on move 12 by opting for the pin 12...Re8? instead of 12...Bxf4. Still, after White castled queenside with 14.O-O-O?, both sides launched pawn storms at opposing kings. You pushed forward on the queenside while White targeted your g7-square with 16.Qh6.

White overextended with 17.Nf4??, but your defensive retreat 17...Kh8?? opened the door for kingside danger. White offered a bishop on f5 to crack your king, and taking the bait with 18...gxf5?? removed the critical guard on g7, allowing immediate mate with 19.Qg7#.

review.turning_point: After White played 18.Bf5??, your position was still winning with 18...Ng8, but capturing the piece with 18...gxf5?? surrendered your kingside shield and allowed 19.Qg7#.
review.focus: Prioritize king defense over capturing pieces when an opponent's heavy pieces are aimed at your castled position, avoiding reflexive captures like 18...gxf5.

When Black checked with 6...Bb4+, your response 7.Bd2 stepped into a pin against your king along the e1-b4 diagonal, but after trades on d2 you maintained a solid position and pushed forward in the center with 9.e5.

After 9...dxe5 10.dxe5, Black targeted your advanced central pawn with 10...Ng4. Here you needed to neutralize the pressure, with 11.Bb5 creating a pin on the c6-knight to defend your center. Instead, you played 11.h3, leaving the e5-pawn loose to 11...Ngxe5, which cost you a pawn and shifted the momentum completely to Black.

Black traded down with 12.Nxe5 Nxe5 and defended their knight with 13...Qe7 after your 13.Qe2. Looking to kick the piece away, you tried 14.f4?!, but 14...Nxc4 won your bishop on c4, leading directly to your resignation.

review.turning_point: The decisive slip was 11.h3, which failed to protect the e5-pawn and allowed Black to seize the initiative with 11...Ngxe5.
review.focus: Before playing pawn kicks against active enemy pieces, always calculate the immediate captures they threaten, as seen before 11.h3.

Instead of capturing it with 4.Bxb6, you played 4.b3?? to guard the b2-pawn, letting them safely retreat with 4...Qc7.

The game continued with Black expanding on the queenside and fianchettoing. After trades on the b-file left you up a pawn, Black tried a discovered attack against your rook on a1 with 9...Ng8??, but retreating all the way home handed the initiative right back to you. You calmly protected the rook with 10.Ra2.

After rooks were exchanged on a5, you blocked the check with 13.Nd2 and held an extra pawn with a very comfortable position. Unfortunately, the blitz clock ran out after Black played 13...Bh6, ending the battle prematurely.

review.turning_point: The major missed opportunity was 4.b3??, where 4.Bxb6 would have simply won Black's queen on the spot.
review.focus: Always check what your opponent's move stopped defending before making your own move, especially when an enemy piece is sitting on an attacked square like on 4.b3.

sections.text: You faced the English Opening and adopted a solid setup. When White went for 11.Nxd5?, you responded accurately with 11...Nxd5!, gaining comfortable central control. You pushed a bit too eagerly with 13...e4?, which released your grip and gave White counterplay after 14.Nd4, but you quickly recovered your footing by activating your pieces.

The turning point arrived when White played 19.Rd1?? to pin your bishop on d6 to the rook on d8. You immediately punished the oversight with 19...Qe5!, targeting both h2 and the unprotected bishop on b5. After White played 20.f4, you captured the loose piece with 20...Qxb5 to go a full piece ahead.

From there, you converted smoothly. You scooped up queenside pawns with 21...Qxb2 and 22...Qxa3, created a dangerous passed a-pawn, and pushed it down the board. After trading down into a winning endgame, your pawn safely reached 38...a1=Q just as White ran out of time.

review.turning_point: White blundered with 19.Rd1??, walking into the dual attack 19...Qe5!, which won the bishop on b5 outright.
review.focus: Look out for premature central breaks like 13...e4?, which gave up your advantage; developing with 13...Nc6 would have kept White under pressure.

Kxf7??, you punished Black's exposed king with 12.Qf3+!, executing a fork against the king on f7 and the knight on e4 before snapping it up on 13.Qxe4. review.focus: Double-check candidate forcing moves for simple tactical refutations before executing sacrifices, as seen on 17.Qxe5+.

review.headline: A sharp kingside battle slips away on the queenside

sections.text: You handled the Queen's Gambit Declined solidly through the opening, but things grew tense when White probed your kingside. After 17.e4, you looked to double rooks with 17...Raf8?, missing a chance to strike first with 17...Nxe4. That allowed White to trade knights on f6 and clamp down with 19.e5, pushing your bishop back to g7.

White overextended with 21.g4?, and you seized the moment with 21...Rf3!, landing a strong outpost that set up a pin on the f2-pawn. When White blundered with 23.Bf5?, you correctly captured with 23...exf5! to win a piece. However, after 24.Qxf3, you closed the position with 24...f4? instead of opening lines toward White's king with 24...fxg4.

With the kingside locked up, White activated their pieces on the opposite wing. After 25.Ba3 and a sequence of queenside pawn breaks starting with 29.a4, your defenses were stretched too thin. White penetrated down the a- and c-files, eventually winning your d5-pawn with 34.Rxd5.

review.turning_point: After winning the exchange on f3, your decision to play 24...f4 allowed White to shut down your counterplay and freely target your queenside.
review.focus: Look for dynamic pawn breaks when you have attacking chances, such as playing 24...fxg4 instead of closing the file with 24...f4.

The game heated up when White invaded on the queenside. After 26.Rxc6, you created counterplay on the open a-file, though 28...Ne6 handed White strong kingside pressure. After 29.Nh5, you defended with 29...Qf7, which established a pin on the f6-bishop along the f-file. White misstepped with 30.Nxf6, allowing your strong 30...Qxf6, which set up a skewer against White's queen and the f3-knight.

You fell behind in material, but White gave you a lifeline with 37.Rxd4. You jumped on it with 37...Nxe5, winning back the knight and fighting all the way to an equal rook-and-knight endgame. Unfortunately, while defending actively, 48...Kg6 walked straight into a decisive fork with 49.Re6+, winning your knight on d6.

review.turning_point: After battling back to an even endgame, 48...Kg6 walked into 49.Re6+, losing the knight and leaving White with a winning king-and-pawn endgame.
review.focus: Always check your king's alignment with loose pieces before stepping forward, especially in endgames like move 48...Kg6.

sections.text: You handled the Scandinavian opening cleanly, gaining space and developing naturally with 3.Nc3 and 4.d4. When your opponent castled queenside with 12...O-O-O, you rightly targeted their king, pushing forward with 13.a4, 14.a5, and 16.a6 to fix weaknesses around their structure.

The game was balanced as Black struck back in the center with 18...e5. Instead of maintaining active tension with 19.c5, you retreated with 19.Qd1??, allowing Black to drop a fork with 19...e4, hitting both your bishop on d3 and knight on f3.

You tried to counterattack with 20.c5, where Black responded with 20...exd3, which created a discovered attack along the e-file against your rook on e1. You found the best practical reply in 21.cxd6!, but after the rooks were traded with 22.Rxe8 Rxe8, you were down a piece and chose to resign.

review.turning_point: 19.Qd1?? surrendered the initiative and allowed 19...e4, winning a piece by forking your minor pieces.
review.focus: When your opponent breaks in the center with moves like 18...e5, calculate concrete tactical threats instead of passively retreating with 19.Qd1.
